title: Attic & Roof Deck Spray Foam Insulation
metaTitle: Attic & Roof Deck Spray Foam St. George, UT | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Roof-deck and attic-floor spray foam for St. George, Washington City & Hurricane homes. Cut summer AC bills. Free on-site quote: 844-967-5247.
summary: Roof-deck and attic-floor spray foam that shuts down the single hottest surface on a Washington County home, pulling attic temperatures down and taking real load off the air conditioner from May through September.
intro: An unvented asphalt-shingle or tile attic in St. George can hit 140 to 150 degrees on a July afternoon, and every duct run, air handler, and sheet of drywall sitting under that roof deck absorbs it. Fiberglass batts laid across the attic floor slow that heat down, but they don't stop it, and they do nothing for the ductwork and equipment that's actually sitting inside the superheated space. Spray foam gives you two different ways to solve that problem, and St. George Foam installs both, depending on how your attic and roofline are built.

The first option is a roof-deck application: closed-cell foam sprayed directly to the underside of the roof sheathing, which pulls the entire attic into the conditioned envelope of the house. Once the attic is inside the thermal boundary, the HVAC equipment and duct runs living up there are no longer baking in triple-digit air  -  they're sitting in roughly the same temperature as the rest of the house. For homes with attic-mounted air handlers, which is most production-built houses in St. George, Washington City, and Hurricane, that single change often does more for cooling performance than any other upgrade on the property.

The second option is an attic-floor application: foam sprayed across the ceiling plane itself, sealing top plates, can-light housings, plumbing stacks, and duct boots while keeping the attic vented and outside the thermal envelope. It costs less than a full roof-deck conversion and it's the right call for a lot of homes  -  particularly older construction where the roof framing, decking condition, or budget doesn't line up with a full conversion. We walk the attic with every customer before quoting and tell you plainly which approach fits your roof, not just the one that's easier to sell.

We run both approaches as a normal part of the business, on new construction and on twenty-year-old homes where the original fiberglass has settled, been torn up by rodents, or simply never covered the eaves properly to begin with. If a previous installer sprayed foam in your attic and it's not performing  -  too thin at the eaves, missing an ignition barrier, or failing an inspection  -  that's a call we take too; see our spray foam removal and correction work for what that process looks like.
benefits: Pulls attic-mounted HVAC equipment and ductwork inside the conditioned envelope on roof-deck jobs, cutting duct loss
Reduces attic air temperature from the 140-150 degree range down closer to house temperature in summer
Lowers the number of hours your AC compressor runs on peak July and August afternoons
Seals the ceiling-plane leaks fiberglass batts never stop: top plates, can lights, plumbing stacks, duct boots
Keeps attic storage space usable instead of an oven half the year
Closes off common rodent and pest entry points at the eaves and soffit
idealFor: New-construction homes where the roof deck is open before shingles or tile go on
Homes with an attic-mounted air handler and ductwork running through unconditioned space
Tile-roofed homes holding extra radiant heat through the afternoon and into the evening
Older homes where fiberglass batts have settled, shifted, or been damaged and no longer cover the ceiling plane evenly
Additions with new roof framing that need to match the performance of a foam-insulated main house

sections.heading: Roof-Deck vs. Attic-Floor: Which One Fits Your House
body: The right call depends on what's already up there. If ductwork and an air handler live in the attic, a roof-deck conversion usually pays for itself faster because it takes the equipment out of the heat entirely rather than just slowing heat transfer through the ceiling. If the attic is empty mechanically and just holds boxes and the water heater vent, an attic-floor application often gets you most of the comfort gain for a lower price.

Roof pitch and decking condition matter too. Low-slope tile roofs with tight attic clearance are harder to spray evenly at the eaves than a steep-pitch asphalt-shingle roof with full walking room, and that access difference shows up in both the quote and the install timeline. We measure and photograph the attic on every estimate so the recommendation is based on your roof, not a generic number.
bullets: Attic-mounted HVAC or ductwork usually points toward roof-deck
Empty, storage-only attics often do fine with attic-floor sealing
Low-slope tile roofs need extra care and time at the eave line
Budget and roof deck condition both factor into the final recommendation

sections.heading: How the Install Works
body: On a roof-deck job we spray closed-cell foam directly to the sheathing between the rafters, typically two to three inches depending on the target R-value, then apply an intumescent ignition-barrier coating over any foam left exposed to living space per code, since foam by itself isn't a fire-rated finish. Vents get sealed or removed as part of converting the attic to unvented, and any HVAC equipment up there gets worked around carefully so ducts and refrigerant lines aren't damaged during spraying.

On an attic-floor job the crew works the ceiling plane systematically: top plates first, then every penetration  -  can lights, bath fan housings, plumbing vents, duct boots, the attic hatch itself  -  before filling the open floor area. Cure time for both open-cell and closed-cell foam is fast; the space is typically safe to re-enter within hours, and full off-gas of the initial application smell is usually gone within a day or two in St. George's low humidity.

sections.heading: The Full-Service Difference
body: A lot of insulation crews in Washington County do fiberglass batts most weeks and treat spray foam as a side offering. We run dedicated foam crews on residential attics and roof decks every day, which is also why we're comfortable taking on the jobs other companies pass on  -  steep tile roofs, tight attic clearance, additions that have to match an existing envelope, and attics where a previous contractor's foam job needs to be pulled out and redone correctly before we spray.

priceFactors.detail: Roof-deck conversion covers more surface area and typically runs thicker closed-cell foam, so it costs more per square foot than sealing the attic floor alone.
Steep, tight, or low-clearance attics slow the crew down and add labor time compared to a full-height walkable attic.
Foam exposed to living space (like a finished attic or knee-wall storage room) needs an intumescent coating, which adds material and labor.
Pulling out old, damaged, or rodent-contaminated fiberglass before spraying adds a removal step to the job.

priceFactors.factor: HVAC and ductwork in the attic
priceFactors.detail: Equipment and duct runs that need to be worked around, sealed to, or protected during spraying add coordination time.

faqs.q: Do you spray over my old fiberglass insulation or remove it first?
faqs.a: For attic-floor jobs we typically remove damaged, settled, or contaminated fiberglass first so the foam bonds directly to the deck and ceiling plane instead of sitting on top of compromised material. If your existing insulation is in decent shape, we'll tell you honestly whether removal is actually necessary.

faqs.q: Does converting to a roof-deck system void my shingle or tile warranty?
faqs.a: Spraying the underside of the deck doesn't touch the roofing material itself, so it doesn't interact with most manufacturer shingle or tile warranties. We recommend confirming with your specific roofing manufacturer if your home is still under an active roof warranty, just as a formality.

faqs.q: How much hotter is a vented attic than the inside of my house in August?
faqs.a: It's common for a vented attic here to sit 40 to 60 degrees hotter than the living space on a peak August afternoon. A roof-deck conversion is aimed directly at closing that gap since it brings the attic into the conditioned envelope instead of just insulating against it.

faqs.q: Is an ignition barrier always required?
faqs.a: It's required anywhere the foam is exposed to occupied or storage space rather than sealed behind drywall  -  a finished attic room, a knee-wall closet, or an open rafter bay someone could walk into. We include it automatically wherever code calls for it.

title: Closed-Cell Spray Foam Insulation
metaTitle: Closed-Cell Spray Foam Insulation St. George, UT | St. George Foam
metaDescription: High-density closed-cell spray foam for roof decks, exterior walls, crawl spaces & metal buildings in St. George, UT. Call 844-967-5247.
summary: Dense, rigid, R-6 to R-7 per inch spray foam that St. George Foam runs across the toughest applications on our schedule  -  roof decks, exterior walls, crawl space perimeters, rim joists, and metal building interiors  -  anywhere moisture resistance and structural add-on matter as much as R-value.
intro: Closed-cell spray foam is the dense, rigid product in our lineup, curing at roughly R-6 to R-7 per inch  -  close to double the insulating value of open-cell foam for the same cavity depth. That density comes from a tighter cell structure packed with an insulating gas rather than open air pockets, which is also what makes closed-cell resistant to bulk moisture and largely impermeable to water vapor. It's the product we reach for on the jobs where thin-cavity performance, moisture control, or added rigidity actually matter, not just wherever the highest R-value sounds good on paper.

That rigidity is a real, practical benefit on top of the insulation value. A wall or roof deck sprayed with two to three inches of closed-cell foam gains meaningful stiffness beyond what the framing alone provides, which is part of why it's the standard product for pole barns, steel-frame shops, and metal buildings  -  it adds structural contribution at the same time it's controlling temperature and condensation on the panel. We spec closed-cell across residential and commercial work interchangeably; the chemistry doesn't care whether it's going on 2x6 wood studs in a Santa Clara home or steel purlins in a Hurricane warehouse.

On roof decks, closed-cell is usually the right call over open-cell because it's spraying directly against a surface that sees real temperature swings and, occasionally, minor roof leaks before anyone notices them  -  closed-cell's vapor resistance means it won't wick and hold that moisture against the sheathing the way an open-cell application can. The same logic applies below grade at crawl space perimeter walls and at rim joists, where the foam sits close to soil moisture, seasonal grade water, and outside air infiltration all at once.

We keep closed-cell in stock and running on crews every week rather than special-ordering it for the occasional job, which is part of why we can move fast on tight-turnaround commercial work and same-week residential projects without the material lead time other shops run into.
benefits: Roughly double the R-value per inch of open-cell foam, useful where cavity depth is limited
Adds meaningful structural rigidity to stud walls, roof decks, and metal building framing
Highly resistant to bulk water and largely impermeable to water vapor
Reduces condensation risk on cold surfaces like metal roof panels and rim joists
Bonds directly to wood, concrete, and steel without a separate vapor barrier layer
Holds up well in exposed applications  -  crawl space walls, rim joists, roof decks  -  where open-cell isn't recommended
idealFor: Roof decks under tile, metal, or asphalt shingle roofing
Exterior walls where cavity depth is limited and maximum R-value per inch matters
Crawl space perimeter walls and rim joists exposed to ground moisture
Metal building and pole barn interiors needing condensation control
Any application where added structural rigidity is a bonus, not just insulation

sections.heading: Why Density Matters More Than R-Value Alone
body: It's tempting to shop spray foam purely on R-value per inch, but density is really what you're paying for with closed-cell  -  the R-value is a side effect of a cell structure built to resist water, add stiffness, and hold up in exposed, unconditioned, or high-swing-temperature applications. A rim joist or crawl space wall doesn't need R-20; it needs a material that won't degrade sitting a few inches off graded soil through a monsoon season.

That's the calculation we walk customers through when they ask why one part of the house gets closed-cell and another gets open-cell on the same job. It's rarely just a budget decision  -  it's matching the product to what that specific assembly is exposed to.

sections.heading: Where We Run Closed-Cell Across Residential & Commercial Jobs
body: On the residential side, closed-cell shows up most on roof decks, crawl space perimeters, rim joists, and garage ceilings under living space above. On the commercial side, it's close to the default product for metal building interiors, where its direct-to-steel adhesion and vapor resistance solve the condensation problem that plagues uninsulated or fiberglass-blanketed pole barns and warehouses.
bullets: Crawl space perimeter walls and rim joists
Metal building walls, roofs, and purlins
Garage ceilings below finished living space
Exterior walls in tight 2x4 framing where every R-point per inch counts

sections.heading: Installation & Cure
body: Closed-cell is sprayed in lifts, typically an inch to an inch and a half at a pass, to control the exothermic reaction and keep the foam curing evenly rather than overheating in one thick application. A finished thickness of two to three inches is common on roof decks and walls; crawl space and rim joist work is usually sized to the specific R-target rather than a flat number. Full cure is fast  -  the assembly is typically ready to close in or drywall within 24 hours.

priceFactors.detail: Closed-cell is priced by the board-foot; a 3-inch roof deck application costs more per square foot than a 1.5-inch rim joist seal.
Spraying against steel purlins on a metal building involves different surface prep than wood-frame sheathing or concrete foundation walls.
High roof decks or tall metal building walls may require scaffolding or lift equipment that adds to the job cost.
Any closed-cell foam left exposed to occupied space needs an approved coating over it per code.

faqs.q: What's actually different about closed-cell versus open-cell, in plain terms?
faqs.a: Closed-cell is denser, roughly double the R-value per inch, resists water, and adds real stiffness to the assembly it's sprayed into. Open-cell is lighter, cheaper per square foot, and better suited to interior cavities where air-sealing and cost matter more than moisture resistance or rigidity.

faqs.q: Does closed-cell work on metal buildings and pole barns?
faqs.a: Yes  -  it's the primary product we use on metal building interiors because it bonds directly to steel panels and purlins and controls the condensation ('sweating') that's common on uninsulated or poorly insulated metal roofs in this climate.

faqs.q: How thick does closed-cell need to be for my project?
faqs.a: It depends on the application and target R-value  -  roof decks commonly run 2 to 3 inches, rim joists and crawl space walls are often sized closer to 1.5 to 2 inches. We size it during the on-site walkthrough rather than quoting a flat thickness for every job.

faqs.q: Is closed-cell foam a vapor barrier by itself?
faqs.a: At around 2 inches or more it functions as a Class II vapor retarder in most residential applications, which is generally sufficient for our climate zone without needing a separate poly sheet behind it. We'll flag it specifically if your assembly needs anything additional.

title: Open-Cell Spray Foam Insulation
metaTitle: Open-Cell Spray Foam Insulation St. George, UT | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Budget-friendly open-cell spray foam air sealing for St. George & Washington County homes, R-3.5-3.7/inch. Get a free quote: 844-967-5247.
summary: Lighter, more affordable spray foam built for interior wall cavities and attic floors, where air-sealing and sound control matter more than raw density  -  and where St. George Foam specs it deliberately, not as a discount substitute for closed-cell.
intro: Open-cell spray foam cures to roughly R-3.5 to R-3.7 per inch, expanding aggressively into a soft, spongy structure that fills a stud bay or attic floor joist cavity completely, wrapping around wiring, plumbing, and blocking without the pressure buildup that can bow thin drywall or sheathing. It costs less per square foot than closed-cell, and for interior applications that don't need moisture resistance or added rigidity, that lower price isn't a compromise  -  it's the right tool for the job.

The real value of open-cell isn't the R-value on the spec sheet, it's air sealing. Fiberglass batts slow heat transfer but never stop air movement; a house full of batts still leaks conditioned air around every outlet box, top plate, and duct penetration. Open-cell foam closes those gaps directly, which is what actually keeps a St. George house from feeling like it's fighting a losing battle against 105-degree air infiltration all summer.

As a full-service shop we spec open-cell specifically where it earns its place: interior partition walls, attic floors in homes keeping a traditional vented attic, additions with open framing, and as one half of a hybrid system where closed-cell handles the roof deck or exterior envelope and open-cell fills interior cavities for cost efficiency and sound control. We're not trying to upsell every job to closed-cell, and we're not defaulting to open-cell everywhere to save on material either  -  the application dictates the product.

Open-cell also does something batts can't touch: it cuts sound transfer between rooms noticeably. In the open, great-room-style floor plans common in newer St. George and Washington City construction, that shows up as a real, felt difference between a primary suite and an adjacent laundry room, or around a home office and the rest of the house.
benefits: Lower material and installed cost than closed-cell, useful on larger cavity or whole-attic projects
Expands fully into irregular stud bays, around wiring, plumbing, and blocking
Strong air-sealing performance against hot, dry outdoor air infiltration
Noticeably reduces sound transfer between interior rooms compared to batt insulation
Lightweight, non-load-bearing formulation that won't stress ceiling or wall framing
Works cleanly alongside closed-cell in a hybrid system on the same job
idealFor: Interior partition walls between bedrooms, bathrooms, offices, and living spaces
Attic floors in homes keeping a traditional vented attic rather than converting to roof-deck
New-construction interior framing before drywall goes up
Additions and remodels with open wall cavities
Homes pairing open-cell interior walls with closed-cell at the roof deck or exterior envelope

sections.heading: What Open-Cell Is Good At (and Where It Isn't)
body: Open-cell is not a moisture barrier and it's not the product for a roof deck, an exterior-adjacent wall assembly, or a crawl space perimeter  -  those applications belong to closed-cell, and we'll say so plainly during the estimate rather than defaulting to whichever product is on the truck. Where open-cell earns its spot is interior, conditioned-space work where air-sealing and cost efficiency are the priority and there's minimal moisture exposure.

Its soft, flexible cell structure is also a real installation advantage in retrofit walls packed with old wiring and fixtures  -  it conforms around obstructions without the expansion pressure that dense closed-cell can put on thin materials, which usually means a cleaner, faster job in a remodel wall cavity.

sections.heading: Air Sealing and the St. George Cooling Load
body: Washington County's cooling season runs from roughly May through September, with July highs regularly hitting 104-106 degrees. Every unsealed gap in an interior wall or attic floor is a pathway for that heat to work its way toward conditioned space, and it doesn't matter how thick the batt insulation is if the air is moving around it rather than through it. Open-cell foam closes that pathway directly at the top plates, can-light housings, duct boots, and plumbing penetrations that fiberglass simply can't seal.

sections.heading: Hybrid Systems We Build
body: A lot of the homes we work on end up with both products on the same job: closed-cell at the roof deck or crawl space perimeter where moisture resistance and rigidity matter, open-cell filling interior partition walls and attic floor cavities where air-sealing and cost efficiency are the priority. We run both materials on the same crew day, so hybrid jobs don't mean scheduling two separate visits or two separate estimates.

priceFactors.detail: Larger whole-attic or whole-house interior wall projects benefit most from open-cell's lower per-square-foot cost.
Standard 2x4 or 2x6 interior partitions install differently than deeper attic floor joist bays.
Open, unfinished framing before drywall is faster and less expensive to spray than a retrofit cavity accessed through an opened wall section.
Jobs combining both products are priced by area and product, not a single blended rate.

faqs.q: Is open-cell foam worse than closed-cell, or just different?
faqs.a: It's different, not worse. Open-cell trades density and moisture resistance for a lower cost and excellent air-sealing performance, which is exactly what interior walls and vented attic floors need. Closed-cell is the right call where moisture resistance or rigidity matters  -  open-cell is the right call where it doesn't.

faqs.q: Will open-cell foam work in our humid monsoon weeks?
faqs.a: Yes  -  St. George's monsoon window from mid-July into September is short, and outside of it ambient humidity stays low. For interior wall and attic-floor applications, open-cell's moisture permeability isn't a functional issue in this climate the way it can be in genuinely humid regions.

faqs.q: Can you mix open-cell and closed-cell on the same job?
faqs.a: Regularly. It's one of the most common configurations we install  -  closed-cell at the roof deck or crawl space, open-cell in interior partition walls and attic floor area, sprayed by the same crew in one visit.

faqs.q: How much sound reduction does open-cell actually give us between rooms?
faqs.a: It's a noticeable, felt difference rather than a lab number most homeowners care about  -  open-cell in an interior partition wall meaningfully quiets voices, plumbing noise, and footfall transfer compared to a standard fiberglass batt wall.

title: Exterior Wall Spray Foam Insulation
metaTitle: Exterior Wall Spray Foam Insulation St. George, UT | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Exterior wall spray foam for new builds & remodels in St. George, Santa Clara, Ivins & Hurricane, UT. Open- or closed-cell systems. 844-967-5247.
summary: Open-cell or closed-cell foam sprayed into exterior wall cavities on new-construction framing and open-wall remodels, sized to hit IECC Climate Zone 3B performance targets without over-building the assembly.
intro: Exterior wall performance is where a lot of a home's cooling load gets decided, and it's also where the choice between open-cell and closed-cell matters most, because the wrong call in a 2x4 or 2x6 cavity either underperforms or wastes money. We spray exterior walls on new-construction framing before drywall goes up, and on remodels and additions where walls are opened for other work, sizing the product and thickness to actually hit Climate Zone 3B targets rather than defaulting to whatever's cheapest or whatever's on the truck that day.

Open framing is the reality of this work  -  spray foam is installed into open stud bays, not blown or injected behind finished drywall. That means the strongest fit is new construction, where we're on-site between the framer and the drywaller, and remodels or additions where walls are already opened up for electrical, plumbing, or window work. If your walls are closed and finished, exterior wall spray foam generally isn't the retrofit path; we'll say so directly rather than quoting a job that doesn't make sense for your house.

Washington County sits in IECC Climate Zone 3B, and production and custom builders across St. George, Santa Clara, and Ivins are increasingly speccing spray foam into exterior walls specifically to hit code more comfortably and future-proof against tightening energy requirements. We work directly with builders and GCs on this, scheduling around framing and rough-in inspections rather than treating spray foam as an afterthought bolted onto the tail end of a build.

On remodels, exterior wall foam shows up most often on garage-to-living-space conversions, room additions, and whole-house re-insulation projects where a homeowner is already gutting walls for other reasons and it makes sense to upgrade the envelope while everything is exposed.

sections.heading: New Construction vs. Remodel Wall Cavities
body: New construction is the cleanest application: framing is complete, electrical and plumbing rough-in is done, and the crew has full, unobstructed access to every stud bay before insulation inspection. We coordinate directly with the builder's schedule so the spray happens in the same window a batt subcontractor would normally be on-site.

Remodel work is more variable  -  it depends entirely on how much of the wall is actually open. A gutted addition wall behaves like new construction; a wall opened only around a single window replacement doesn't have enough exposed cavity to make spray foam practical, and we'll tell a homeowner that upfront instead of quoting a job that doesn't fit the scope of what's actually accessible.

sections.heading: Meeting Climate Zone 3B Code
body: St. George falls under IECC Climate Zone 3B, which sets minimum insulation and air-sealing performance for new construction and major renovations. Spray foam's air-sealing properties help exterior wall assemblies meet code with less reliance on separate house-wrap taping and caulking details, and closed-cell in particular can help thinner wall assemblies hit target R-values without adding framing depth.

sections.heading: Working With Your Builder or GC
body: We work as a direct sub to builders and general contractors across Washington County, scheduling around framing completion and coordinating with the rough-in inspection so insulation goes in at the right point in the build sequence. If you're a GC managing multiple lots or phases, we can talk through a standing schedule rather than quoting each house one at a time  -  reach us at 844-967-5247 or josh@contractorschoiceagency.com.

priceFactors.detail: Closed-cell costs more per square foot but hits higher R-value in the same 2x4 or 2x6 cavity depth.
Whole-house new construction pricing differs from a single addition wall or partial remodel section.
Fully open new-construction framing installs faster than a remodel wall with partial obstructions or existing utilities.

faqs.q: Can you spray foam into my existing finished exterior walls without opening them up?
faqs.a: Generally no  -  exterior wall spray foam is installed into open stud bays, not injected behind finished drywall. If your walls are closed, we'll talk through whether a different service, like attic or crawl space work, gets you more comfort improvement for the dollar.

faqs.q: Does spray foam help pass a Climate Zone 3B energy code inspection?
faqs.a: Yes, when it's sized correctly for the wall assembly. We coordinate directly with builders around rough-in and insulation inspections so the install lines up with what the inspector is checking for.

faqs.q: Open-cell or closed-cell for exterior walls  -  which do you recommend?
faqs.a: It depends on cavity depth, budget, and whether the wall is exposed to more moisture than a typical interior condition. We'll walk the framing with you and make a specific recommendation rather than a blanket answer.

faqs.q: How do you coordinate timing with our framing crew?
faqs.a: We schedule directly with the builder or GC's timeline, typically after framing and rough-in inspection are complete and before drywall starts. We work with several builders across St. George, Santa Clara, and Ivins on a recurring basis.

title: Crawl Space Spray Foam Insulation
eyebrow: Perimeter Walls, Rim Joists & Moisture Control
metaTitle: Crawl Space Spray Foam Insulation St. George, UT | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Seal crawl space perimeter walls & rim joists with closed-cell spray foam in St. George, Hurricane & LaVerkin, UT. Call 844-967-5247.
summary: Closed-cell spray foam applied to crawl space perimeter walls and rim joists, sealing the vented crawl space out of the thermal envelope and cutting off one of the more overlooked energy-loss points in a Washington County home.
intro: A lot of homes in Washington County still have vented, unconditioned crawl spaces built to an older standard  -  open foundation vents letting outside air, dust, and moisture move freely underneath the house. That worked fine as a construction method for decades, but it means the floor system above sits directly on top of whatever temperature and humidity happen to be under the house, and it means any ductwork running through the crawl space is losing conditioned air into unconditioned space with every cycle.

We seal that off by spraying closed-cell foam directly onto the crawl space perimeter foundation walls and rim joist band, effectively moving the crawl space envelope from the floor system down to the foundation wall itself. It's the same building-science logic as a roof-deck conversion, applied at the bottom of the house instead of the top: bring the space inside the thermal boundary instead of just insulating the floor above it.

Rim joists deserve their own mention because they're the single most commonly missed insulation gap in a typical Washington County home. It's the band of framing sitting directly on top of the foundation wall, running the full perimeter of the house, and in most standard construction it gets a thin strip of fiberglass at best  -  full of gaps at every joist bay. Sealing it with closed-cell foam closes one of the largest continuous air leaks in the entire building envelope.

Homes closer to the Virgin River bench around Hurricane and LaVerkin, and anywhere grade slopes toward the foundation after a monsoon downpour, see more crawl space moisture than homes further up the bench toward St. George proper. Closed-cell's resistance to bulk water makes it the right product for this application regardless of location, but it matters even more where seasonal moisture is a bigger factor.

sections.heading: Sealed vs. Vented Crawl Spaces
body: A vented crawl space lets outside air move freely underneath the house, following older building code that assumed venting prevented moisture problems. In practice, in a hot desert climate, venting just means the crawl space temperature tracks outside conditions almost exactly  -  hot in summer, and pulling humid monsoon-season air in during storm weeks. Sealing the perimeter with closed-cell foam and closing off the vents moves the space inside the building's thermal and moisture boundary instead.

sections.heading: Rim Joists: The Overlooked Leak Point
body: Standard construction typically insulates rim joists with a thin fiberglass strip cut to fit each joist bay, if it's insulated at all consistently. Every gap between those cut pieces is a direct air path from outside to the floor system above. We treat the rim joist band as its own dedicated pass on every crawl space job, spraying it continuously rather than leaving it as an afterthought around the perimeter sealing work.

sections.heading: What's Involved in a Crawl Space Job
body: We start by assessing crawl space height, access point, existing insulation condition, and any moisture or grading issues that should be addressed before spraying. Old, sagging, or contaminated batts get pulled out, foundation vents are typically sealed or mechanically closed, and closed-cell foam is sprayed across the perimeter wall and rim joist in a continuous pass sized to the target R-value for your specific crawl space depth.

priceFactors.detail: Priced by the linear footage of foundation wall and the crawl space's height, since taller crawl spaces have more wall area to cover.
Low-clearance crawl spaces slow the work down compared to a full-height crawl space a crew member can stand in.
Pulling out old, sagging, or moisture-damaged batts before spraying adds a removal step.
Adding or replacing a ground vapor barrier alongside the foam work is often recommended and priced separately.

faqs.q: Do you insulate the crawl space floor or the perimeter walls?
faqs.a: For sealed-crawl-space conversions we spray the perimeter foundation walls and rim joist band, not the ground itself, which is the current best-practice approach versus insulating between floor joists in a vented crawl space.

faqs.q: Will sealing my crawl space cause a moisture or mold problem?
faqs.a: When it's done correctly  -  including a ground vapor barrier and proper foundation vent closure  -  a sealed crawl space typically runs drier than a vented one, since it's no longer pulling in outside humidity during the monsoon window. We assess ground moisture and grading as part of every quote.

faqs.q: How do you handle existing HVAC ductwork in the crawl space?
faqs.a: We work around active ductwork carefully during spraying and can flag any obvious duct leaks or disconnections we notice while we're under the house, even though duct sealing itself isn't part of the insulation scope.

faqs.q: My crawl space has very low clearance  -  can you still do the work?
faqs.a: In most cases yes. Low-clearance crawl spaces take longer and get priced accordingly, but our crews regularly work in tight, low-height crawl spaces across older Washington County construction.

summary: Spray foam for attached garages, detached shops, RV garages, and home workshops across Washington County, aimed at turning a space that's unusable half the year into one you can actually work, park, or train in year-round.
intro: Garages and shops in St. George get treated as an afterthought by whoever built them, and it shows every July when the space hits temperatures that make it unusable for anything beyond parking a car. Newer subdivisions around Desert Color, Sun River, and Little Valley increasingly include RV garages and oversized bays built for hobbyists, and even those get built with minimal or no insulation as a standard spec  -  the builder assumes it's a storage space, not somewhere anyone plans to spend time.

We treat garage and shop insulation as its own category because the use cases are so different from a standard living space. A car collector wants stable temperature swings to protect paint and interiors. A home gym conversion needs the space usable at 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. without running a portable AC unit at full blast. A workshop with power tools and glued-up projects needs consistent humidity and temperature more than a bedroom does. We size the insulation package to what the space is actually going to be used for.

Attached and detached buildings get different treatment. An attached garage under living space or sharing a wall with conditioned rooms usually gets the ceiling and shared walls sprayed to control heat and sound transfer into the house. A detached shop or pole-barn-style outbuilding gets treated more like a small commercial structure  -  walls, roof deck, and any roll-up door framing all factor into the plan since there's no adjacent conditioned space doing any of the work for you.

Metal roll-up doors are one of the biggest weak points in almost every garage we quote, whether it's a two-car attached garage or a four-bay detached shop. We address that directly during the walkthrough rather than insulating everything around the door and leaving the single largest surface area on the wall untouched.

sections.heading: Attached Garage vs. Detached Shop
body: An attached garage shares at least one wall or a ceiling with conditioned living space, so insulating the shared surfaces cuts both heat gain in the garage and heat and sound transfer into the house. We typically spray the ceiling (especially with a bedroom or living space above), the shared interior wall, and sometimes the garage door header area, depending on layout.

A detached shop or outbuilding doesn't get any help from an adjacent conditioned space, so the whole building envelope  -  walls, roof or ceiling, and door framing  -  needs to be addressed for the insulation package to actually change how the space performs. We scope these more like small standalone buildings than an add-on to the house next door.

sections.heading: Metal Roll-Up Doors and Other Weak Points
body: A standard uninsulated steel roll-up door is one of the largest single surfaces of poor thermal performance in a typical garage. We can't spray foam directly onto a moving door panel, but we treat the surrounding framing, header, and any adjacent wall sections carefully, and can point you toward insulated door panel options as a companion upgrade where it makes sense for the project.

sections.heading: Turning a Garage Into Usable Space Year-Round
body: Most of these projects come down to one question: does the homeowner want the garage or shop to function as real usable space, or is it staying a hot box for storage? Once that's answered, the insulation package follows from it  -  a home gym conversion gets treated more aggressively than a garage that's just parking two cars and holding a workbench.

faqs.q: Can you insulate a garage that already has drywall up?

faqs.q: Will this help with noise from my garage gym or shop equipment?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly on shared walls and ceilings between the garage and living space  -  spray foam noticeably reduces sound transfer compared to an uninsulated wall or ceiling cavity.

faqs.q: Do you insulate detached shops without any existing insulation at all?
faqs.a: Regularly  -  a lot of our shop and pole-barn work is the first insulation that building has ever had, since many detached structures get built with no thermal package as standard.

faqs.q: What about the garage door itself?
faqs.a: We don't spray the moving door panel, but we address the surrounding framing carefully and can point you toward insulated door panel replacement as a companion upgrade if the door itself is the weak point.

title: Commercial & Metal Building Spray Foam
metaTitle: Commercial & Metal Building Spray Foam St. George, UT | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Metal building & commercial spray foam in Washington County, UT. Condensation control, thermal & noise dampening. Call 844-967-5247.
summary: Closed-cell spray foam engineered for metal buildings, warehouses, and commercial shops across Washington County  -  stopping panel condensation, cutting HVAC load in large-volume spaces, and dampening monsoon noise on metal roofs, work most residential-only crews in this market don't take on.
intro: Metal buildings in St. George have a problem most owners don't fully understand until they see it firsthand: sweating steel. A metal roof or wall panel has almost no thermal mass, so it tracks outside air temperature almost instantly. On a clear desert night, even after a 105-degree day, radiant cooling can drop that panel's surface temperature below the interior dew point, and by early morning it's dripping condensation onto whatever's stored underneath  -  inventory, equipment, hay, vehicles, tools. This isn't a rare edge case here; it's a predictable, recurring problem tied directly to how the desert climate swings between day and night.

Spray foam solves it in a way fiberglass blanket-and-screw systems, still the default in a lot of pole barn and ag building construction, don't: closed-cell foam bonds directly to the metal panel, eliminating the air gap where condensation actually forms in the first place. There's no vapor barrier to fail, no blanket sagging away from the panel over time creating new gaps, and no seams for humid interior air to reach the cold steel surface behind the insulation.

This is a category of work most spray foam crews in this market don't take on at all  -  a lot of outfits here are built around residential attics and walls and simply don't run the crew size, lift equipment, or scheduling flexibility that commercial buildings need. We run it as a core part of the business, not a side job, which means we can quote and staff a 20,000 square foot warehouse the same week we're doing a two-car garage.

The building types we work most often are self-storage facilities, RV and boat storage buildings, agricultural and ranch buildings, steel-frame shops, and pole barns across Washington County  -  anywhere metal panel construction meets a desert climate that swings 30 to 40 degrees between afternoon peak and pre-dawn low, even in the middle of summer.

sections.heading: Why Metal Buildings Sweat in the Desert
body: It seems counterintuitive that a building in one of the hottest parts of Utah has a condensation problem, but it's precisely the desert's dry-air, high-diurnal-swing climate that causes it. Low humidity means clear skies most nights, and clear skies mean strong radiant cooling of exposed metal surfaces  -  a roof panel can radiate heat to the night sky fast enough to drop well below the ambient air temperature, and well below the interior dew point of a building holding any moisture at all from equipment, vehicles, livestock, or simple occupancy.

Once that panel surface drops below dew point, moisture condenses directly on the steel, and without a thermal break or vapor-sealed insulation layer between the panel and the interior, that water finds its way onto whatever's stored below  -  and over years, onto the steel framing itself, where it becomes a corrosion problem rather than just a nuisance.

sections.heading: Direct-to-Metal Application
body: We spray closed-cell foam directly onto roof panels, wall panels, and purlins from the interior, building up to the target thickness for the building's use case  -  a climate-controlled shop calls for more R-value than an ag building that just needs condensation stopped. The direct adhesion means there's no gap for interior humidity to reach the cold steel behind the insulation, which is the actual mechanism that ends the sweating problem, not just insulating value on a spec sheet.

sections.heading: Commercial Timelines and Crew Scheduling

For occupied buildings, we can schedule around business hours, work in sections to keep part of the facility operational, or run overnight and weekend passes when that fits the owner's operation better. Reach us at 844-967-5247 to talk through scheduling for your specific building and use case.

faqs.q: Does spray foam adhere to rusted or older metal panels?
faqs.a: It depends on the extent and type of surface condition  -  light surface rust is usually fine after prep, but heavier corrosion may need treatment or panel repair first. We inspect the substrate as part of every commercial estimate before quoting.

faqs.q: How exactly does spray foam stop the condensation we're seeing?
faqs.a: By bonding directly to the metal panel, closed-cell foam eliminates the air gap and vapor pathway that lets interior humidity reach the cold steel surface where condensation actually forms. It's a mechanical fix, not just added R-value.

faqs.q: Can you work around our business hours or ongoing operations?
faqs.a: Yes  -  we regularly schedule commercial jobs in sections, overnight, or on weekends to keep occupied buildings operational during the install. Tell us your constraints when you call and we'll build the schedule around them.

faqs.a: Both, depending on the building's condensation and thermal goals. Roof-only passes are common for basic condensation control on ag and storage buildings; occupied shops and offices usually get walls included for comfort as well.

title: Spray Foam Removal & Correction
eyebrow: Fixing Jobs Other Crews Got Wrong
metaTitle: Spray Foam Removal & Correction St. George, UT | St. George Foam
metaDescription: Spray foam removal & correction in St. George, UT - off-ratio foam, failed inspections, odor complaints fixed right. Call 844-967-5247.
summary: St. George Foam removes and corrects failed spray foam installs from other contractors - off-ratio chemistry, wrong product for the application, missing code-required coatings, and lingering odor complaints - and re-sprays it right.
intro: Spray foam is chemistry sprayed on-site by a technician, and when the process goes wrong, it goes wrong in specific, identifiable ways. The most common failure is off-ratio mixing: spray foam is a two-component system, an A-side and a B-side pumped through heated hoses at a precise ratio and temperature, and if that ratio drifts - from a miscalibrated rig, a bad hose heater, or an inexperienced technician not catching it mid-spray - the foam never cures properly. It stays tacky, spongy, or crumbly instead of setting into the rigid or semi-rigid structure it's supposed to have, and it often keeps off-gassing a chemical smell for weeks or months instead of clearing within a day or two like a correctly cured job.

The second common failure is the wrong product for the application - open-cell sprayed on an exposed roof deck where it should have been closed-cell, or foam sprayed directly over an active roof leak that trapped moisture against the decking instead of solving the problem. The third is a code miss: foam left exposed in living space without the required ignition-barrier coating over it, which shows up as a failed inspection, sometimes not caught until a home sale or a remodel opens the space back up.

We get called into these situations by homeowners who smell something wrong months after their spray foam install, by inspectors flagging a fail on a new-construction or remodel job, by home buyers whose pre-purchase inspection turned up bad foam in the attic or crawl space, and by general contractors who inherited a subcontractor's work mid-project and need it corrected before they can move forward. It's a distinct skill from a fresh install - diagnosing what actually went wrong, removing it without damaging the structure underneath, and re-spraying to a standard that will actually pass inspection and stop the complaint.

This isn't a side offering bolted onto our install business. We treat correction work as its own discipline, because the diagnostic step matters as much as the removal - spraying new foam over a problem that was never actually identified just buries the issue again.

sections.heading: How to Tell Your Spray Foam Job Went Wrong
body: A properly cured spray foam job stops smelling within a day or two and sets into a firm, stable structure that stays bonded to whatever it was sprayed onto. When something's wrong, it usually shows up as one or more of a handful of recognizable signs, and homeowners are often relieved to learn there's a name for what they're dealing with rather than assuming it's just how spray foam always smells or feels.
bullets: A tacky, soft, or spongy surface that never fully firms up, sometimes weeks after the install
A persistent chemical odor that doesn't fade after the first few days
Visible gaps, voids, or thin spots, especially at eaves, corners, and rim joists
Foam pulling away or delaminating from the framing, decking, or metal panel it was sprayed on
A crumbly, friable texture that flakes apart rather than holding its shape
Missing ignition-barrier coating over foam that's exposed in living or storage space

sections.heading: What Removal & Correction Involves
body: We start with an on-site assessment - checking cure state, coverage, thickness, and whether the issue is isolated to one area or spread across the whole assembly. Off-ratio and failed foam gets mechanically removed by scraping and cutting rather than chemically dissolved, since that protects the roof decking, wall framing, or metal panel underneath from further damage. Removed material is hauled off, the substrate is inspected and cleaned, and we re-spray with the correct product, ratio, and thickness for the application - closed-cell where the original job wrongly used open-cell, proper ignition-barrier coating where it was missing the first time.

sections.heading: Working With Inspectors and Home Sales
body: When correction work is tied to a failed inspection, we coordinate directly with the inspector on what's needed to pass re-inspection and schedule the re-spray to line up with that timeline. For home sales, we can document the correction with photos and a written scope for the buyer, seller, or their agent, which is often exactly what's needed to move a stalled closing forward when bad foam turns up during a pre-purchase inspection.

priceFactors.detail: A localized bad section costs less to correct than a full roof deck or whole-attic removal.
Hand-scraping a small area differs in cost from mechanical removal across a large assembly.
Larger removal jobs generate more material that has to be hauled and disposed of properly.
If moisture damage or rot is found under the failed foam, that repair is scoped separately before re-spraying.
Reinstalling drywall, trim, or an ignition-barrier coating after correction adds to the total scope.

faqs.q: How do I know if my spray foam job was actually done wrong?
faqs.a: The clearest signs are a chemical smell that doesn't fade after a few days, foam that stays soft or tacky instead of firming up, visible gaps or voids, or a failed inspection. If any of that sounds familiar, an on-site assessment can tell you definitively rather than guessing.

faqs.q: Is the smell from bad spray foam actually dangerous?
faqs.a: A short-lived odor during the first day or two of a correctly cured job is normal and expected. A strong smell persisting for weeks or months usually points to off-ratio or under-cured foam, and we'd recommend having it assessed rather than assuming it will eventually clear on its own.

faqs.q: Will you work with my home inspector or the seller's contractor?
faqs.a: Yes - we regularly coordinate with buyers' inspectors, sellers' agents, and the original installing contractor's paperwork when a home sale is on hold over a bad spray foam finding.

faqs.q: Do you have to remove the entire installation, or just the bad section?
faqs.a: Only the bad section, whenever that's technically possible - we assess coverage and cure state across the whole assembly first and remove only what's actually failed rather than defaulting to a full tear-out.
